newsitem.title: MEXICO: Telephone firms hook up in Mexico's Monterrey.
newsitem.headline: Telephone firms hook up in Mexico's Monterrey.

text.p: Rival telephone firms competing with former Mexican monopoly Telefonos de Mexico (Telmex) began placing calls for customers on Friday in Mexico's second city of Monterrey.

The process was marred, however, because only a third of the phones in this city of 3 million were able to connect with a phone company other than Telmex. The remainder of the city will have the option in two weeks.

"The opening of Monterrey's market will not take place in all the (telephone) centrals today, but will only enter in a third of the centrals," Carlos Casasus, the Federal Telecommunications Commission, told reporters here after meeting with state Gov Benjamin Clariond.
His statements followed confusion by some Monterrey residents surprised by the delay, although a piecemeal opening had always been scheduled for this industrial city.
Telmex rivals will be able to connect to its local network in the second third of Monterrey beginning on Jan. 18 and with the remaining part of the city on Jan. 24, Cassasus said.

The two heavy-hitters in the Mexican market besides Telmex are Avantel, an alliance of Grupo Financiero Banacci and MCI Communications, and Alestra, a union of Grupo Alfa, holding company VISA-Bancomer and AT&T Corp..

The race for divying up Mexico's long distance phone market began in the central city of Queretaro, but Monterrey is considered the crown jewel in initial competition, until the new companies invade Mexico City on April 1.

Greater Monterrey area's more than three million residents, with about 520,000 phone lines, have been bombarded with advertisements from principal competitors for their long distance peso in recent weeks.

New telephone companies have said they hope to make the public aware of their new options in telephone carriers, in an attempt to improve the weak exodus from Telmex seen in Queretaro, where only about a third of callers chose to fill out ballots giving them a chance to subscribe to a carrier other than the former state-run monopoly.
